verdict: ENRICH events/proposition-13.md, section 'The 2026 Revolt Wave' (county-level framing, NACo's 2020-2026 action tally, and the elimination-campaign status with Ballotpedia/Census as the checkable primaries; NACo as compiler and origin only). claim_grade: Source tier (EDITORIAL §4c): Tier 2 - NACo is the membership and lobbying association of US counties; the report argues explicitly for county fiscal autonomy ('Local fiscal autonomy is a bedrock of our democratic system'), so it is advocacy-body origin, never support. Author Jonathan Harris (Director, Research) is a practitioner-author not on sources/audit/people-tiers.json; judged by the rubric as Tier 2. (The scanner's 'Tier-3' label is not the wiki scale.) Claim grades: tallies of state actions and the ~$29.8bn two-year cost = B at best (NACo analysis of NCSL database plus fiscal notes, with NACo's own inference of who bears cost; the endnotes say so; table counts do not reconcile, see uncertainties). Census-derived tax-structure figures (state share of property tax about 3%, sales/gross receipts and income taxes exceeding property tax by $140bn and $111bn in 2022) = A when cited to the Census table I re-derived. ACS/CPI real-terms figures (+57% nominal, +9% real, effective rate -18%) = B, NACo calculation from named primaries I could not fetch; the arithmetic is internally consistent. 26% of county revenue and 41% of property tax going to schools = C/B, NACo's own adjustment of Census Individual Unit data. Elimination-campaign status = A/B from Ballotpedia plus the official ND result (Ballotpedia is an aggregator, B); NACo's assertion adds nothing beyond it. Normative framing ('state preemption', 'one-size-fits-all') = C, advocacy position.

headline_claims_with_locators.figure: At least 168 state property tax actions in 40 states and DC, Jan 2020 - Jun 2026
headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'From January 2020 to June 2026, state legislatures enacted at least 168 property tax actions in 40 states and the District of Columbia.' (Key Takeaways; State Legislation, endnote vi)
headline_claims_with_locators.nacos_source: 'NACo analysis of National Conference of State Legislatures, State Tax Actions Database (2020-2025); NCSL State Ballot Measures Database (2020-2025); and additional sources from NACo's own research.' Appendix I map has the state-by-state list.

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'Nearly three-quarters (72%) of the property tax actions passed from 2020 through June 2026 - 121 out of 168 - increased relief measures in some way. The largest share (65) created or modified a property tax exemption in 20 different states.' (State Legislation)
headline_claims_with_locators.nacos_source: same NCSL base. Relief = exemptions, credits, refunds and 'other relief' (circuit breakers, deferrals, aid).

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'Over the past six years, four states (Colorado, Iowa, Ohio and North Dakota) and the District of Columbia passed legislation to impose a rate or levy limit or to make an existing one more restrictive.' (State Legislation). Iowa SF 2472 (2026) cited as a 'new 2 percent levy limit' for counties; North Dakota HB 1176 as a 3% levy limit.
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Scanner said 'four states'; the report says four states plus DC. The data table gives 5 actions in 5 states. Cost of all rate/levy changes nearly $2.6bn (table: $2,594.58m).

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'Ten states implemented changes to property assessments (Alabama, Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, South Dakota and Wyoming), which alter the calculation of property values.' Examples: Alabama 7% limit with reset on sale or major renovation (HB 73); Arizona commercial assessment ratio 18% to 16% (SB 1093); South Dakota 3% limit on growth of AGGREGATE assessed value of owner-occupied single-family homes in each county (SB 216). Assessment changes 'estimated to cost counties at least $200 million annually' (State Legislation). Table row: 'Assessment Ratio/Limit' 15 actions, 10 states, $395.81m.
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Scanner's '10 assessment-limit changes' conflates limits with ratio changes; the ten states include ratio changes, and Colorado/Wyoming/California items are not described individually.

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'State legislative actions were calculated to reduce local tax revenues by $15.3 billion in the fiscal year after passage, followed by another $14.5 billion in the next fiscal year - not including the 34 ballot measures and six other bills which passed and do not have fiscal notes.' Split (endnotes viii-x, NACo inference): about 16% borne solely by local governments, 25% by states (reimbursement, possibly temporary), 58% shared.
headline_claims_with_locators.nacos_source: Fiscal notes compiled by NCSL, supplemented by NACo; allocation of burden is NACo's own inference. $15.3bn + $14.5bn = $29.8bn (checked).

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'Since 2024, at least 15 states have discussed some form of property tax elimination, though none have passed any legislation to do so.' (State Legislation; endnote xv cites only 'NACo Research, 2026'). Key Takeaways: legislators drove it in nine states, governors in Florida, North Dakota and Texas, and 'Ohio, Michigan and South Dakota have all seen citizen-led movements to eliminate the property tax with a ballot measure.'
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Scanner wrote 'within two years'; report says 'since 2024'. Only the named states are identified; the other nine are not listed in the text. Replacement proposals named: Georgia fees (HR 1114 / HB 1116), Indiana and Kansas sales-tax-exemption repeal (HB 1288, HCR 5014), higher sales/consumption taxes in Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Wyoming; North Dakota oil fund.

headline_claims_with_locators.figure: Median bill +57% nominal, +9% real, effective rate -18%
headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'While the median property tax bill increased by 57% ($1,168) from 2010 to 2024, most was due to inflation and real property taxes only increased by 9% ($189), using 2010 dollars. Over the same period, the calculated effective tax rate actually declined by 18%.' (Key Takeaways; Political Vulnerability). Endnote xvii: 'Median real estate taxes paid increased from $2,043 in 2010 to $3,211 in 2024'; endnote xxi: 'estimated effective property tax rate is calculated by dividing aggregate real estate taxes paid by the aggregate value of owner-occupied housing units... should not be interpreted as a statutory property tax rate.' Chart note: ACS 1-year estimates, no 2020 release. Same section: per-capita personal income +82%, home prices 'doubled', state and local sales taxes +107%, income taxes +106% vs property taxes +70% (2010-2024; Census Quarterly Summary of State and Local Tax Revenue, endnote xxiii).
headline_claims_with_locators.nacos_source: Census Bureau American Community Survey 1-year, 2010 and 2024 (median real estate taxes paid); BLS CPI-U annual averages; BEA personal income via FRED.
headline_claims_with_locators.note: I re-computed: 3,211/2,043 = +57.2%; 3,211 deflated by CPI-U (2010 218.1, 2024 313.7, from memory, BLS not reachable) = $2,232, i.e. +$189 or +9.3% on $2,043. Consistent. The 'median bill' is the ACS median of real estate taxes paid by owner-occupied units, not a tracked-house bill; the -18% effective rate is aggregate-to-aggregate.

headline_claims_with_locators.figure: Political vulnerability: 26% of county revenue, under 2% of state general revenue
headline_claims_with_locators.wording: Key Takeaways: 'over one quarter (26%) of county government revenue but less than 2% of state general revenue and 0% of federal revenue.' Body (What Do Property Taxes Pay For?): 'Counties invest over $740 billion each year... Over one quarter of this investment ($200 billion, or 26%) is only possible because of property taxes.' Also: 'approximately 3% of revenue going to states' (Introduction); property tax about 'three-fifths of all county tax revenue'; 41% of property tax revenue goes to schools (NACo adjusted allocation, endnote xxvii).
headline_claims_with_locators.nacos_source: Census of Governments: Finance, individual unit file 2022, NACo-adjusted (reallocations for county-run school systems and city-county consolidations; excludes CT, RI, DC).
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Denominator is ambiguous: 'revenue' in the takeaway, '$740bn investment' (expenditure) in the body. Census Table 1 check: state governments collected $21.6bn of the $649.0bn total property tax (3.3%), which is 0.7% of state general revenue ($3,051.8bn) and 1.5% of state taxes ($1,473.6bn), so 'under 2%' holds on either base.

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'In 2022, residents and businesses paid $140 billion more in state and local sales and gross receipts taxes and $111 billion more in state and local income taxes than in property taxes.' Endnote xxii: Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances via Urban Institute; 'aggregate tax collections... rather than taxes paid by a representative household.'
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Verified from Census Table 1: sales and gross receipts $789.24bn - property $649.03bn = $140.2bn; individual $600.62bn + corporate $159.66bn - property = $111.2bn (so the $111bn includes corporate income tax; the text says 'income taxes'). Note the 'residents and businesses paid' wording is NACo's, the Census figure is collections.

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: 'In an analysis of 292 local ballot measures related to property taxes which were introduced from 2020 to 2025, 246 (84%) passed.' (endnote xxix: Ballotpedia, coverage limited to the 100 largest cities, state capitals and all of California and Virginia; only 26 raised an exemption and two proposed any decrease). 'No state to date has had a property tax elimination ballot pass... North Dakota voters were directly asked in 2024... voted down by a very large margin: 63-37.'
headline_claims_with_locators.note: ND result confirmed on Ballotpedia: No 63.46% (225,889), Yes 36.54% (130,038), 'Results are officially certified'.

headline_claims_with_locators.wording: Cost of providing government services 49% vs cost of living 44%, 2010-2024 (BEA state and local implicit price deflator vs CPI-U); county property tax revenue, adjusted for population and service-cost growth, rose by less than 1% a year on average 2002-2022.

'all states except five - Hawaii, Kansas, Minnesota, New Hampshire and Tennessee - set significant limits on counties' ability to raise revenue through property taxes' (endnote xiv: 'NACo Research, 2026'; Appendix II ranks each state's limits on property, sales and income taxes; severity bands defined at the foot of Appendix II).

headline_claims_with_locators.figure: Descriptive mechanics NACo states for relief types
headline_claims_with_locators.wording: Homestead exemption: 'Typically applied only to homesteads... so shifts the burden to businesses, second-home owners and renters.' Credits/refunds likewise shift burden 'to other non-eligible homesteads, businesses, second-home owners and renters.' (Property Tax Relief Measures box). 'Local governments tend to bear the costs of these traditional limits.'
headline_claims_with_locators.note: Descriptive, no cited evidence; same burden-shift point the wiki already carries from the Tax Foundation (origin only).

content_summary.state_examples_named: Wyoming: 50% exemption up to $3m for owners 65+ who have paid property tax 25+ years (HB 3 and HB 45) and 25% exemption on first $1m of market value of owner-occupied residential property (SF 49). Texas: general school homestead exemption $100,000 to $140,000 (SB 4); senior/disabled additional exemption $10,000 to $60,000 (SB 23); together about $2bn a year. Indiana SEA 1 (10% homestead credit up to $300 in 2026). Delaware senior credit $400 to $500 (HB 250). Alabama HB 73, South Dakota SB 216, Iowa HF 718 (2023) and SF 2472 (2026), North Dakota HB 1176. All named as NACo's descriptions; bill numbers not checked against legislatures.
content_summary.history_endnotes_leads_for_other_pages: Endnote v cites two Tier 1 sources not fetched: Bethany Paquin, 'Chronicle of the 172-Year History of State-Imposed Property Tax Limitations', Lincoln Institute (Oct 2024), with a long dated list of 1970-1980 limits (1978 California assessment limit and rate limit; 1980 Massachusetts rate and levy limit; and so on), and Rita Jefferson, ITEP (Jul 2025), 'Anti-Tax Revolts Backfire'. Endnotes xi and xiii cite Langley and Youngman, 'Property Tax Relief for Homeowners', Lincoln (2021). T1 may cite these directly for the 'Legacy and Spread' section instead of NACo.

primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.north_dakota: Initiated Measure 4 (2024), citizen-initiated constitutional amendment prohibiting taxes on assessed value of real or personal property (bond levies excepted), with state replacement payments, defeated 5 Nov 2024: No 63.46% (225,889), Yes 36.54% (130,038). Opponent estimate of replacement need $1.329bn a year (Keep It Local ND, quoted on Ballotpedia). Note NACo lists North Dakota under 'governor-led' for 2025-26 discussion and separately for the 2024 citizen vote; the 2025 HB 1176 (3% levy limit; credits) is the enacted outcome.
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.ohio: Citizen initiative 'Eliminate and Prohibit Taxes on Real Property' (AxOHTax) cleared for signature gathering by Attorney General (title approved 9 May 2025) and the Ballot Board (14 May 2025). Ballotpedia, citing Signal Ohio (5 Jun 2026): the committee suspended its 2026 ballot effort and will gather signatures for 2 Nov 2027. Not on Ohio's 2026 ballot (Ballotpedia lists only Issue 3, voter ID). Consistent with the Lincoln explainer's 'fell short of making the ballot' already in the wiki. Lincoln working paper (Walczak, 2026; already in wiki as research/lincoln-ohio-property-tax-alternatives) prices the Ohio proposal at about $21.1bn a year.
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.michigan: AxMITax (initiated constitutional amendment prohibiting taxation of real and personal property and requiring 60% voter approval for voter-approved taxes) filed Jan 2025; founder announced 22 May 2026 that it had not collected the 446,198 valid signatures within the 180-day window; status 'Not on the ballot' (deadline 6 Jul 2026).
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.south_dakota: Initiated constitutional amendment (Mueller, Frye-Mueller, Smith; approved for circulation 3 Nov 2025) to eliminate property taxes and impose a retail transaction tax ($1.50 on purchases of $15 or more, 10% under $15); needed 35,017 signatures by 3 Feb 2026; status 'Not on the ballot'. Separately a referendum on SB 245 (a state fund for homeowner property tax reduction) is also listed as not on the ballot. NACo's text separately credits SD with a 3% aggregate-assessment limit (SB 216).
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.florida: HJR 203 (eliminate all non-school taxes on homestead property; legislatively referred) passed the House 80-30 on 19 Feb 2026 and is listed 'Not on the ballot' (news reports: died in Senate Appropriations when the session ended 13 Mar). DeSantis then called a special session (announced about 27 May); the outcome was CS/HJR 1F on the Nov ballot as Amendment 3 ($150k then $250k non-school homestead exemption, non-homestead cap 10% to 5%), which the wiki already carries. Note Amendment 3 is a large exemption, not an elimination. NACo's 'governor-led' attribution is supported by news reports.
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.texas: Governor Abbott's reelection plan (Dec 2025, restated Apr 2026) would let voters end school district property taxes on homesteads by constitutional amendment, with local spending growth limited to population growth plus inflation or 3.5% (whichever lower); state officials estimate about $8.6bn a year; no change possible before the Legislature meets in 2027 (secondary news reports only; no Texas measure on the Nov 2026 ballot).
primaries_checked_for_elimination_campai.november_2026_ballot_overall: Ballotpedia's property-tax hub lists 13 statewide 2026 measures in 7 states (Florida 2 and 3; Georgia 1; Louisiana 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10; North Carolina levy-limit amendment; Oklahoma SQ 847; Tennessee 2; Wyoming Initiative 1); Louisiana Amendment 4 was defeated on 16 May, leaving 12 on 3 Nov. None of them eliminates local property taxes. Tennessee Amendment 2 only bars the General Assembly from creating a STATE property tax (Tennessee has none), which is easy to misread as an elimination measure. Massachusetts (2028) and Ohio (2027) are the listed future potentials. Matches the count already on places/wyoming.md.

proposed_edits.position: New fourth paragraph, placed immediately after the Oklahoma/Iowa paragraph whose last sentence reads exactly: 'The Tax Foundation's survey of the November ballots reads the assessment-limit measures as shifting burdens onto non-favoured property and the levy-limit model as the "neutral" alternative; that is the think-tank's own judgement, but it matches the mechanism described above, under which a limit on collections rather than on assessed values leaves the base intact and the relative tax on land and buildings undistorted.[22]'
proposed_edits.draft_content: The National Association of Counties, which speaks for the governments that levy and depend on the tax, counted at least 168 state property-tax actions in 40 states and the District of Columbia between January 2020 and June 2026; 72 per cent were relief measures (exemptions, credits, refunds), only four states and DC tightened rate or levy limits and ten states changed assessments, and the actions with fiscal notes were put at about $29.8 billion in lost local revenue over the two fiscal years after passage, of which NACo infers about 16 per cent falls on local governments alone and 25 per cent on states.[23] (NACo's own tally, from the National Conference of State Legislatures database and fiscal notes; a counties' lobby, so origin only.) The same report counts at least fifteen states that have discussed outright elimination since 2024 without enacting it. The checkable record agrees: North Dakota's Measure 4 (2024) was defeated 63.5 to 36.5 per cent, Michigan's initiative did not gather its signatures, South Dakota's was not on the ballot, and Ohio's campaign moved to 2027; none of the twelve property-tax measures still on the 3 November 2026 ballot eliminates local property taxes.[24][25]
proposed_edits.sources_to_add: [23] NACo, 'State Policy Trends: Property Tax Reform 2020-2026' (Jonathan Harris, 30 Oct 2026), naco.org URL above - used as the origin of the 168-action tally, the 72% relief share, the ~$29.8bn two-year estimate and the 'at least 15 states' count (Tier 2 association of counties; origin only, not support; read in full; HTML page, no PDF; the cost allocation is NACo's inference; its appendix table counts 163 actions and $28.4bn so the headline figures are not reproducible from the published table). [24] Ballotpedia pages for North Dakota Initiated Measure 4 (2024) (certified result), Michigan Prohibit Property Taxes Amendment (2026), South Dakota Eliminate Property Taxes ... Initiative (2026) and Ohio Eliminate and Prohibit Taxes on Real Property Initiative (2027) (B-claim aggregator; the Ohio and Michigan dates trace to Signal Ohio 5 Jun 2026 and AxMITax's 22 May 2026 announcement). [25] Ballotpedia 'Property taxes on the ballot' (B-claim). T1 should prefer the North Dakota Secretary of State certified result and the Ohio Attorney General initiative list if they can be fetched; I did not reach them.

proposed_edits.position: One added sentence after the Lincoln sentence ending exactly: '...and describes a locality that leaves its rate unchanged as values rise as producing "a silent tax increase".[15]'
proposed_edits.draft_content: On NACo's calculation from American Community Survey data, the median real-estate tax paid by US homeowners rose 57 per cent in nominal terms between 2010 and 2024 ($2,043 to $3,211) but only 9 per cent after adjusting for consumer prices, while the aggregate effective rate (taxes paid divided by owner-occupied home value) fell about 18 per cent as home values roughly doubled; the figures cover a different period from Lincoln's and are a county lobby's own arithmetic.[23]
proposed_edits.caution: This is the 'silent tax increase' point the brief was asked about, but it cuts the other way from the metaphor: NACo's numbers say bills rose faster than prices only in the sense of a slower real-terms rise, while rates fell, i.e. the pressure is a base (value) effect. Use as origin attribution only; do not use it to support the Lincoln claim. The primary (ACS table B25103, CPI-U) was not reachable, so a T1 who can fetch it should cite the primary.

uncertainties: NACo is Tier 2 (association of counties). Every NACo-originated figure must be attributed as NACo's count or calculation; only Census-derived items (state share of property tax ~3%, $140bn and $111bn comparisons) were independently re-derived from the Census Table 1 workbook, and the workbook's column layout (total, blank, state, local per geography) was inferred from the arithmetic (total = state + local checks for US and Alabama).

Internal inconsistencies in the report: (a) text says 168 actions but the 'Since 2020, Most State Actions Have Focused on Exemptions...' table's counts sum to 163; (b) text says 65 exemption actions in 20 states, table says 63 in 19 states; (c) the table's fiscal impacts sum to $28.43bn versus the text's $15.3bn + $14.5bn = $29.8bn ('nearly $30 billion'); (d) 121 of 168 = 72.0% but the table categories for relief do not add to 121 on either exemption count (118 or 120); (e) rate/levy limit: text 'four states and DC', table '5 actions, 5 states'; (f) 26% is 'of county revenue' in the takeaway and 26% of a $740bn 'investment' in the body. T1 should carry only the headline numbers attributed to NACo, or avoid the ones that do not reconcile.

'$30 billion' covers only actions with fiscal notes; 34 ballot measures and 6 bills are excluded, and costs are estimated by NCSL or NACo, and are 'to any level of government'. The state-vs-local split is NACo inference ('When this information is not explicitly available, we infer...').

The 15-state elimination count rests on 'NACo Research, 2026' with no list; only twelve states are named in the text (Ohio, Michigan, South Dakota, Florida, North Dakota, Texas, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Wyoming). Not reproducible.

ACS median taxes ($2,043; $3,211), CPI-U adjustment and the 18% effective-rate decline could not be checked against the Census API or BLS (key required / 403). My arithmetic check used CPI-U annual averages from memory (2010 218.056; 2024 313.689).

The Michigan and Ohio status details are secondary: Ballotpedia cites AxMITax's own announcement and Signal Ohio. The Ohio Attorney General and Secretary of State pages were not fetched. Texas and Florida elimination-plan status rests on WebSearch summaries of news reports (Texas Tribune, KERA, Washington Times, NBC Miami), not read pages; the Florida Amendment 3 detail is already carried on the Prop 13 page from official sources.

Scanner discrepancies to correct before T1: 'four states' is four states plus DC; '10 assessment-limit changes' is ten states with assessment changes including ratios (15 actions); '15 states within two years' is 'since 2024'; 'Tier-3' is not the wiki scale (use Tier 2); '26% of county revenue' has an unstable denominator; '~$30bn' is $29.8bn excluding ballot measures; 'Jonathan Harris, 30 Oct 2026' is correct (page shows 'Oct 30, 2026' and article:published_time 2026-10-30; modified 2026-10-31).

The report is advocacy for county fiscal autonomy and state preemption concerns; its 'political vulnerability' thesis and 'one-size-fits-all' language are opinion. Nothing in it addresses land value taxation or land versus improvements; its Georgist relevance is as context (what the revolt wave actually enacted: mostly homestead exemptions that, in NACo's own words, shift burden to renters, businesses and second-home owners, plus a few levy/assessment limits). The wiki should not imply NACo supports or discusses LVT.

No PDF exists for the report on naco.org; Infogram chart data and the Appendix I per-state table and Appendix II/III lookup were not extracted into numbers (Appendix III text rows are in the saved text file). Appendix I's per-state cost table could be gotten by loading the Infogram embeds if T1 needs state-level figures.
